segments.text: Hello.
Day six.
Nearly a week.
You might be starting to feel it.
Longer stretches where you don't think about it at all.
A bit of pride, quietly.
And that's exactly when a particular passenger tends to speak up.
You met it on the night of Day Xero.
Today it gets its own session, because it's the most convincing one on the bus.
It says, "Just one."
And notice how well it argues.
"You've done nearly a week.
You've proved you can stop.
So one won't matter.
You've earned it.
You can stop again tomorrow."
It takes the thing you're proud of and uses it as the reason to undo it.
Here's what it leaves out.
The gap has been closing for six days.
One cigarette doesn't feed a pleasure.
It reopens the gap.
And then the gap asks again, a little while later, with a much better argument, because now it's "just one more."
It isn't really offering you one.
It's offering you the first one.
So when it shows up, you don't argue.
You play the tape forward.
Let's do that now, slowly.
Take a breath, in a way that feels comfortable for you.
Imagine you said yes.
Picture the first few seconds.
Be honest about them.
There might be relief.
Now keep the tape running.
Ten minutes later.
What are you feeling?
That evening.
Is it one?
The next morning, when you wake up.
What's the first thing you want?
And a week from then.
Where are you?
Now come back.
Right here, six days in, with none of that having happened.
Notice how that feels in your body.
That steadiness is yours.
The thought only ever shows you the first few seconds.
You've just watched the whole thing.
And you don't have to take my word for what those first few seconds are worth.
You checked.
In the prep week, there was one you had with your full attention.
Before it, you guessed how good it would be.
Afterwards, you said how good it actually was.
In a moment, both of those answers will be on your screen.
Have a look at the distance between them.
That's what "just one" is selling.
One honest thing before you go.
If you ever do have one, a slip doesn't undo anything.
The most useful thing is to get straight back to your plan, right now, not tomorrow.
Most people who quit for good had slips, or several tries, along the way.
But you don't need a slip to learn this lesson.
You already ran the experiment.
So today, when "just one" turns up, greet it like someone you recognize.
Then play the tape to the end.
Tomorrow is one week.
I'll see you there.
